newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Foreign doctors ready to advise Yeltsin heart team.
newsitem.headline: Foreign doctors ready to advise Yeltsin heart team.

text.p: The Kremlin is bringing in top Western heart specialists to advise Russian doctors preparing for President Boris Yeltsin's bypass operation.
The presidential press office said in a statement on Friday that two top German cardiologists -- offered by Chancellor Helmut Kohl -- would join the Russian team of experts.
The German government named the two as Axel Haverich, director of a clinic for heart surgery at Hanover's Medical Technical College, and Thorsten Wahlers who also worked there.

Russian media said on Thursday that pioneering U.S. heart surgeon Michael DeBakey would join the team. DeBakey, of Baylor College of Medicine in Houston, Texas, said he had not been approached, but would be happy to help if asked to do so.
The specialists will decide around September 28 when to operate on Yeltsin, who was re-elected for a second four-year term in July.
Doctors have said he needs a relatively simple bypass, in which a vein or artery is removed from one part of the body and grafted into the heart area to improve the flow of blood.
Yeltsin, 65, had two heart attacks last year. He broke a long Kremlin tradition of secrecy on medical issues early this month when he said he would have an operation.
The revelation prompted a wave of articles in Russian newspapers, some of them still clearly relishing the freedoms which arrived at the end of the Soviet era.

Papers printed detailed graphics of ailing hearts, interviews with top doctors and speculation about who would take the reins when the president had his operation and who would hold the "red button" which controls Russian nuclear arsenal.

An article in the weekly Argumenty i Fakty, called simply "The President's Heart", answered technical medical questions about bypass surgery. "Ninety to 96 percent of heart bypass operations are successful," it said happily.

But although by Western standards the Kremlin has so far been extremely sparing with details of Yeltsin's health, some newspapers said on Friday that the openness and the talk of who would succeed him were overdone.
The president had a right to privacy, they said.
The liberal daily Izvestia, using Cold War language to highlight a new issue, said the media had gone too far.
"Of course the health of the head of state is not just a medical question, but also a political one," the paper wrote.
"But at the same time it is difficult to avoid the idea that a natural preoccupation with this question has turned into gross interference in the president's internal affairs."
In Soviet days Moscow used the phrase "interference in internal affairs" as a catch-all reason to veto resolutions or complain about action from the "imperialist" West.
Izvestia, one of the president's main backers during the campaign for July's presidential election, said Russia had to work out a balance between public curiosity and tactlessness.

"A sick person, even if he works as a president, remains a human being and regardless of high office, has the right...to demand an attitude towards himself which meets the norms of civilised society," the paper said.
The government newspaper Rossiiskaya Gazeta said speculation about who should take charge of Russia was inappropriate.

"They started playing patience after (Yeltsin) fell ill, trying to guess who would be in charge...instead of wishing for the earliest possible recovery, which is appropriate for this situation," it said.
